title: Kalmijn & Leopold (2019): Multiple-Choice Quiz
instructions: Choose the single best answer. Distinguish the first and second parental deaths, immediate transitions and later changes, communication modes, and what the observational models can establish. The explanations refer to the linked source segments.

items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the overall findings?
options: Contact increased more persistently after the first death; after the second, the rise was brief and ties faded over time.
Every family experienced steadily rising conflict and continuously falling contact after either parent died.
Death order and elapsed time made no difference: both contact measures and conflict followed the same constant pattern.
After the second death, both contact measures remained permanently above their levels while the parents were alive.
items.answer: Contact increased more persistently after the first death; after the second, the rise was brief and ties faded over time.
items.explanation: The abstract describes a longer-lasting increase after the first parent died, partly explained by ties to the surviving parent. After the second death, the reported increases were short-lived and sibling relationships faded in the longer term. This is an average pattern in the study, not a prediction for every family. The abstract's brief description of an initial conflict increase should not be read as establishing statistical significance.

items.prompt: Why did the solidarity hypothesis predict a larger contact increase after the first parent's death?
options: The first parent to die was assumed to be the mother, whose absence always brings siblings together.
Losing the first parent was expected to remove all rivalry and end every dispute between siblings.
Joint contact with and support for the surviving parent could create extra occasions for siblings to meet.
Siblings experiencing a second parental death were automatically removed from every part of the study.
items.answer: Joint contact with and support for the surviving parent could create extra occasions for siblings to meet.
items.explanation: Hypothesis 2 concerns an additional family-network pathway: siblings may meet while coordinating or jointly providing support to the surviving parent. Hypothesis 3 separately predicts mediation through contact with and support to that parent. The reasoning is distinct from mutual support between siblings themselves.

items.prompt: What did Hypothesis 4, derived from kinkeeping theory, predict?
options: Conflict would rise permanently after the second death because siblings would compete for the vacant family role.
After the second death, sibling contact would eventually fall below its level before the death.
Support to the surviving parent would cease immediately after the first death, leaving contact unchanged.
While either parent survived, every sibling relationship would remain continuously active and equally close.
items.answer: After the second death, sibling contact would eventually fall below its level before the death.
items.explanation: The last parent can occupy a position that connects siblings and their own families. If that position is not fully replaced, contact may gradually decline after an initial increase following the second death. This is a hypothesis about a long-term contact pattern, not a claim that all siblings permanently sever ties.

items.prompt: Which description matches the analytic respondent sample?
options: All 8,161 initial respondents were observed without attrition in each of the four survey waves.
The analysis included 2,601 respondents who lost a parent and 1,211 who experienced no parental death.
The same 10,367 sibling dyads supplied complete conflict and contact measurements at every wave.
There were 3,812 respondents: 1,211 experienced parental death and 2,601 formed the comparison group.
items.answer: There were 3,812 respondents: 1,211 experienced parental death and 2,601 formed the comparison group.
items.explanation: The final respondent sample comprised an event group of 1,211 and a comparison group of 2,601. The expanded data contained 10,367 unique sibling dyads for contact and 6,186 for conflict before the outcome-specific modeling restrictions. These dyad counts are distinct from respondents and dyad-year observations. Conflict questions covered at most two selected siblings.

items.prompt: How were the two contact outcomes measured?
options: Any contact in the previous three months was coded as present or absent and combined across communication modes.
Face-to-face and phone contact were combined into a five-point closeness score averaged across all siblings.
Past-year frequencies were converted to approximate annual contact days and logged separately for the two modes.
Device records supplied monthly durations for every call, letter, and email exchanged directly by the siblings.
items.answer: Past-year frequencies were converted to approximate annual contact days and logged separately for the two modes.
items.explanation: The seven past-12-month categories were recoded to 0, 1, 4, 12, 52, 104, or 300 contact days per year. Before logging, never was recoded from 0 to 1. Face-to-face contact was separate from the measure called phone contact, which also included letters and emails. Conflict instead concerned the past three months and was dichotomized.

items.prompt: Which description fits the fixed-effects strategy?
options: It related within-unit changes over time and used family-clustered robust standard errors.
It randomly assigned parental death and compared average outcomes between treatment arms.
It used respondents without siblings as controls and estimated only an unchanging sex effect.
It relied on one-time differences between families to estimate stable family characteristics.
items.answer: It related within-unit changes over time and used family-clustered robust standard errors.
items.explanation: The fixed-effects models relate changes in sibling relationships to changes in predictors, with standard errors adjusted for sibling dyads nested in families. Stable differences are absorbed by the fixed effects. This does not remove all time-varying confounding or make the timing of parental death a randomized treatment.
items.source: Models: changes within units and family clustering

items.prompt: In models of the first parent's death, how were observations after the second parent's death handled?
options: They replaced all earlier observations.
They received weights based on parent sex.
They were recoded as pre-first-death data.
They were excluded from those models.
items.answer: They were excluded from those models.
items.explanation: The authors excluded all observations after the second death when estimating effects of the first. This separates the two transitions and means that the first-death findings apply while the other parent was still alive. The second-death analyses use their own model specification.

items.prompt: What happened to the first-death coefficient for sibling face-to-face contact after adding the surviving-parent measures?
options: It rose from approximately .10 to .17, confirming complete suppression by the parent variables.
It fell from approximately .17 to .10, while a positive adjusted association remained.
It and the indirect effect both became exactly zero, establishing complete causal mediation.
It stayed unchanged because neither parent-contact measure was associated with sibling contact.
items.answer: It fell from approximately .17 to .10, while a positive adjusted association remained.
items.explanation: The reduction from about .17 to .10 was statistically significant in the mediation test. Face-to-face contact with the surviving parent provided the clearest contribution; its support index was not independently significant for this outcome. A positive adjusted first-death coefficient remained. This supports partial statistical mediation rather than an established causal sequence.

items.prompt: Which statement matches the authors' approximate interpretation of face-to-face contact after the first death?
options: It rose by about 17%, with no statistically significant decline over the subsequent observed years.
It fell by about 30% immediately and continued to decline at an increasingly rapid rate afterward.
It remained unchanged, while phone, letter, and email contact declined significantly every year.
It showed no transition effect because conflict was the only outcome that changed significantly.
items.answer: It rose by about 17%, with no statistically significant decline over the subsequent observed years.
items.explanation: The unadjusted log-contact transition coefficient was .173, which the authors describe approximately as a 17% increase. This uses the log coefficient as a percentage approximation, not an exact percentage conversion. The duration coefficient was not significant. Phone contact showed a similar positive transition and nonsignificant duration; the other parent remained alive in these models.

items.prompt: What pattern did the fitted contact trajectories show after the second parent's death?
options: Both contact measures declined at a constant rate from the death year, without an initial increase.
Only face-to-face contact briefly increased; phone, letter, and email contact remained unchanged.
Both initially rose, then fell below the predeath level, with the fitted decline becoming less steep.
Both initially fell, then recovered to approximately 30% above the predeath level after seven years.
items.answer: Both initially rose, then fell below the predeath level, with the fitted decline becoming less steep.
items.explanation: The quadratic models combined positive transition estimates, negative linear duration terms, and positive squared-duration terms. The fitted trajectories therefore declined after the initial rise and later flattened. The authors describe about 30% lower face-to-face contact and 15% lower phone contact by the longer-term comparison illustrated around year seven. These are estimated patterns, not a uniform change in every dyad.

items.prompt: How did the authors assess the two conflict hypotheses?
options: Both H5 and H6 were supported: a significant initial increase was followed by a significant long-term decline.
H5's temporary increase was not supported; the long-term decline after the second death was consistent with H6.
Only H5 was supported: conflict rose initially but showed no subsequent decline after the second death.
Neither H5 nor H6 was supported because no transition or duration coefficient indicated a change in conflict.
items.answer: H5's temporary increase was not supported; the long-term decline after the second death was consistent with H6.
items.explanation: The discussion explicitly rejects support for H5 and identifies the declining pattern as consistent with H6. The first death showed no significant conflict change, and the initial increase after the second death was not significant. The significant result was the later decline after the second death, so a positive initial estimate is not evidence of a confirmed temporary conflict surge.

items.prompt: What did the additional analysis suggest about parent sex and the second-death pattern?
options: All second deaths were mothers' deaths, so the authors had no basis for examining parent sex.
Declining contact occurred only when the father died second and was absent when the mother died second.
Mothers' deaths changed conflict alone, whereas fathers' deaths changed contact alone in all models.
Most second deaths were mothers' deaths, but the contact effects did not differ significantly by parent sex.
items.answer: Most second deaths were mothers' deaths, but the contact effects did not differ significantly by parent sex.
items.explanation: In 75% of these cases, the mother died after the father. The authors found no significant interactions of second-death transition or duration with parent sex for either contact measure. They therefore emphasized the position of the second parent rather than attributing the pattern solely to mothers. A nonsignificant interaction does not establish identical effects in every group.
items.source: Additional analysis: death order and parent sex

items.prompt: Why did the authors describe the later pattern as fading rather than deteriorating sibling ties?
options: Competition intensified, producing increasingly frequent conflict despite unchanged contact.
All siblings reconciled, so less conflict demonstrated greater affection and stronger relationships.
Contact and conflict both declined, suggesting less interaction rather than escalating antagonism.
Only measurement error changed, leaving the observed contact and conflict patterns without meaning.
items.answer: Contact and conflict both declined, suggesting less interaction rather than escalating antagonism.
items.explanation: A decline in conflict alone could look like improvement, but the parallel decline in contact suggests that ties became less active. The authors interpret this as fading after the loss of an integrative family member. They did not directly demonstrate either universal reconciliation or worsening hostility.

items.prompt: Which alternative interpretation limits the causal conclusion about the surviving parent?
options: More sibling contact might itself encourage solidarity with and support for the surviving parent.
Random assignment established that parent support always preceded and caused greater sibling contact.
Fixed effects removed every changing confounder, making a reverse direction logically impossible.
The mediation estimates used only cross-sectional differences unrelated to the observed parental deaths.
items.answer: More sibling contact might itself encourage solidarity with and support for the surviving parent.
items.explanation: The authors explicitly acknowledge that sibling contact may promote solidarity with the surviving parent. Their pattern is consistent with the proposed parent-to-sibling pathway but does not rule out the reverse direction. Single-reporter measures, limited conflict measurement, and the Dutch setting also constrain interpretation.

items.prompt: Which mechanism was not directly measured?
options: Past-year face-to-face contact frequencies for the respondent's nonresident siblings.
Who acted as a kinkeeper and which activities they used to organize the family network.
Recent conflicts or disagreements with up to two randomly selected nonresident siblings.
The respondent's frequency of face-to-face contact with the surviving parent over the year.
items.answer: Who acted as a kinkeeper and which activities they used to organize the family network.
items.explanation: The long-term results fit kinkeeping theory, but the study lacked direct measures of kinkeeper identities and activities before and after death. Who organized gatherings or assumed a vacant role therefore remains a mechanism for future research, rather than an observed mediation pathway in these data.
